title: Seven Doors of a Leaf
logline: In a cinnamon-peeling shed, quality is judged by smell, touch and sound as much as by sight, a grade decided before a word is spoken.
human_question: When a judgement is made through several senses at once, what does each one actually contribute?

premise.story: Workers in a cinnamon-peeling shed peel, scrape, roll and grade bark, testing quills by smell, touch, sound and sight as they work.
premise.place: A cinnamon-peeling shed in the southern low country.
premise.experience: The viewer follows a single quill from raw bark to graded product, noticing how many different senses are folded into knowing a good one without anyone explaining it.

concept_links.why: The source's six doors, each admitting only its own kind of object, sight only colour, smell only scent, touch only texture and temperature, describe, in doctrinal terms, exactly the separate channels a peeler is drawing on and combining without naming them.
The source ties each sense to a physical base the mind depends on; watching workers rely on fingers, nose and ear in turn is a concrete, human version of that dependence.
The source's account of smell and taste as blended, present-moment mixtures fits how a peeler judges a quill, not by comparing memories consciously, but by meeting the thing itself.

what_camera_could_observe: Bark stripped, scraped and rolled by hand
A peeler lifting a quill to the nose, testing it between the fingers, tapping it
Workers describing, in their own words, how they know a good quill
The finished quills bundled for sale or export
what_must_be_real: The workers' actual skill, pay and working conditions; no staged sensory close-ups that misrepresent an ordinary working rhythm.

possible_arc.opening: Raw bark arrives; the day's peeling begins.
possible_arc.turn: A difficult batch tests the workers' judgement, an unusual smell, an uneven texture.
possible_arc.ending_open: The day's grading is finished, or not, and the quills move on to buyers.

position_hint: opening candidate: a demanding craft using several senses at once, with a real object, a peeling knife or the day's first quill, that could plausibly be where Object 5 is acquired.

requirements: An active cinnamon-peeling shed willing to allow filming during real production
Workers willing to describe, in their own words, how they judge quality
Consent covering the economics of a labour-intensive trade

suggestions.name: Southern coastal cinnamon-growing belt
suggestions.why: Sri Lanka's traditional heartland for cinnamon cultivation and peeling.
suggestions.access_notes: Peeling sheds are often small family operations; access would need direct relationships.
suggestions.verify: A specific shed and willing workers are unconfirmed.

risks: Exoticising manual labour or reducing it to a sensory showcase
Softening the real economic pressures of the trade into a mood piece
Labour conditions in the cinnamon trade can be difficult and should not be glossed over
drop_if: No shed will allow filming of real, unstaged work
The economics of the trade cannot be shown honestly alongside the craft
Workers do not want their judgement process described on camera

connections.note: Both watch what happens to a skilled, sense-dependent life when the senses themselves are the subject.

unknowns: No participant, access or event has been found or confirmed. Everything above is a research direction.
